feedback: If a learner rejects the tilted unequal-length pair, saying the lines are 'not the same length so not parallel', show two parallel lines of very different lengths and slide the ruler between them — parallel means the gap stays constant / the lines never meet, and length does not matter.

If a learner only accepts horizontal or vertical parallels or an upright right triangle, slowly rotate the same figure and let them watch the ruler gap stay constant or the set-square still fit — the property is preserved when you turn the figure.

If a learner accepts the slowly-converging pair as parallel by eye, have them measure the gap straight across at each end to see that it changes, and extend both lines in the direction they close up to show they would meet (if the meeting point is off the page, the changing gap is still the evidence), showing the eyeball guess was wrong.

If a learner is unsure where the rectangle belongs, have them run the two checks separately — slide the ruler for the constant gap and fit the set-square in a corner — and see that it passes both, so it is recorded as having parallel sides AND a right angle.

If a learner swaps the words, re-anchor each to its check: parallel lines run alongside and never meet (the ruler gap holds); perpendicular lines cross at a right angle (the set-square fits the corner). Have them name the relation while performing the check.
activities.intendedInsight: A property, not the look of a figure, decides the category: a tilted, unequal-length pair is just as parallel as a tidy horizontal pair, and a rotated triangle is still a right triangle if a corner tests at 90 degrees. Properties are independent, so a figure can have both (a rectangle), one, or neither. The question shifts from 'does it look like the book example?' to 'does it pass the test?'
learnerActions: Lay out a mixed tray of shapes and lines including a pair of parallel lines of clearly DIFFERENT lengths tilted off horizontal, a pair that looks parallel but slowly converges, a right-angled triangle rotated so neither leg is horizontal or vertical, a rectangle, and a non-right triangle.

For each pair of sides, test for parallel: slide a ruler along one side keeping it touching, and check whether the gap to the opposite side stays the same, measuring straight across (at right angles to the lines) at two or more places, including near both ends where the lines lie alongside each other, or extend both lines to see whether they would meet.
For each corner you suspect is a right angle, drop a set-square or the square corner of a card into the corner and check whether it fits exactly against both sides.

Record each figure by property, testing the two properties independently: does it have a pair of parallel sides? does it have a right angle / is it a right triangle? A figure may pass BOTH tests (a rectangle has parallel sides AND right angles), just one, or neither — note what each check shows rather than forcing it into a single exclusive box, and only decide after the check, not after a glance.

Say out loud, for at least three figures, which check you used and what it showed (for example: 'I slid the ruler and the gap never changed, so these sides are parallel even though one line is longer' or 'the rectangle passed both — parallel sides and a right-angle corner').
activities.title: Sort the tray: test every figure before you bin it

feedback: If the learner's 'parallel' line visibly converges on checking, point to where the gap changes and ask them to redraw keeping the ruler's reported gap constant.
If the 'perpendicular' line fails the set-square, show the gap between the card's square corner and the line and have them adjust until it fits.
If the learner only draws an upright right triangle, ask them to draw one more tilted so no side is straight across or straight up, then confirm the 90 degree corner is still present.
activities.intendedInsight: Producing parallel and perpendicular lines, and a right triangle in a non-standard orientation, is evidence the learner holds the defining property rather than copying a familiar picture.
learnerActions: Given a line drawn at an angle (not horizontal or vertical), draw a second line parallel to it, then check your own drawing by sliding a ruler to confirm the gap is constant.
Given another angled line, draw a line perpendicular to it, then check with a set-square or square corner that the crossing is a right angle.
Draw a right triangle that stands on its point or sits at an angle, so that neither of the two shorter sides is horizontal or vertical; mark the right angle and verify it with the set-square.
Swap drawings with a partner and test each other's lines and triangle with the ruler and set-square, reporting whether each one passes.
activities.title: Draw it, don't just spot it

feedback: If a learner cannot place a rectangle in the 'both' cell, have them separately test a pair of sides for the constant gap and a corner for 90 degrees, then see both tests pass.
If placements are made by appearance, ask them to demonstrate the check for one figure in each cell before moving on.
activities.intendedInsight: Properties combine: a figure can have parallel sides, a right angle, both, or neither, and each property is decided by its own independent check.
learnerActions: Set up a two-way sorting grid: one axis 'has parallel sides / no parallel sides', the other 'has a right angle / no right angle'.
Place each figure from a mixed set into the correct cell, including shapes that belong in the cell with BOTH parallel sides and a right angle (such as a rectangle).
For each placement, state the check you used and keep the ruler and set-square to hand so you can re-test any figure a classmate questions.
activities.title: Sorting grids for mixed properties

feedback: If a learner relies on the card to decide a figure's classification, redirect them to run the check on the figure itself, since the card only reminds them what the words mean.
activities.intendedInsight: A quick visual anchor helps keep 'parallel' and 'perpendicular' straight, but naming is not the same as verifying — the figure in front of you still has to pass the ruler or set-square test.
learnerActions: Keep a small reference card where pointing to a pair of sides shows 'parallel: always the same distance apart, never meet' and pointing to a corner shows the 90 degree square for 'perpendicular / right angle'.
Use the card to settle vocabulary disputes during the sorting and drawing tasks, then return to the physical check to confirm the actual figure.
activities.title: Quick reference card for the two words
